passage:
School counsellor's note, Thursday.
Yash (Class 10) came in today on his own. After Friday's annual day, where he danced a solo, a senior in the corridor laughed and said he "moved like a broken robot". Yash has replayed that line, by his own count, "about a hundred times". When I asked about other reactions, it took him a while: his friend Aadhya made him a card, the music teacher asked him to perform at the district event, and several juniors asked him to teach them. He listed these flatly, as if they didn't count. He said, "They're just being nice." I asked him to write each comment, kind or unkind, on a separate slip and bring them next week. We will look at them together. I'll also check in with his class teacher.

qa.q: What did the senior say about Yash's dance?
qa.a: That he "moved like a broken robot".

qa.q: Why does Yash dismiss the kind reactions as "just being nice"?
qa.a: The mocking line felt like a threat to how he sees himself, so it seems true and important, while the praise seems polite and easy to wave away.

qa.q: Why might writing each comment on a separate slip help Yash?
qa.a: Seeing every comment laid out, one unkind next to many kind ones, lets him weigh them fairly instead of replaying one line.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel if Aadhya knew Yash saw the card as "just being nice"?
qa.a: Aadhya might feel a little hurt that a sincere card didn't reach Yash, and want him to know it was meant.

grounding: It shows a teenager replaying one mocking comment for days while shrugging off warm praise.

passage:
Sunday night
Posted my guitar cover on the class group yesterday. 26 people replied. Gautam said it gave him goosebumps. Riddhima said I should do a whole album. Even Sir sent a thumbs-up.
And one person, Karan from 10C, wrote "lol cringe voice".
I have read that comment maybe fifty times. I read the nice ones once. I keep hearing my voice crack on the high note and thinking he's right, it's cringe, everyone was just being polite.
Mumma said, "Twenty-five against one, Jaya." I know. It doesn't feel like twenty-five against one. It feels like one.
Deleting the video tomorrow maybe. Or not.
- Jaya

qa.q: What did Gautam say about the cover?
qa.a: That it gave him goosebumps.

qa.q: Why does one comment feel bigger to Jaya than twenty-five kind ones?
qa.a: The mocking comment touches Jaya's worry about the voice crack, so it feels like a threat and a hidden truth, while the praise feels like politeness. 😔

qa.q: What could Jaya do before deciding to delete the video?
qa.a: Reread all the kind replies slowly, notice that one person is not 'everyone', and wait a few days before deciding.

qa.q: How might Gautam feel if Jaya deleted the video?
qa.a: He might be confused and a bit sad, since he truly enjoyed it and said so.

grounding: It shows a teenager replaying one mocking comment and brushing off many warm ones, which shakes self-worth.

passage:
The Independence Day function at the government school in Nabha ended at noon, and by evening Amandeep, fifteen, was still thinking about it. She had recited her Punjabi poem in front of the whole village. The sarpanch had shaken her hand. Her teacher had said, "You made me cry." Jatin had shouted "Superstar!" from the back.
But while she was walking off the stage, a boy near the tractor trolleys had called out, "Slow down, grandma, it's not a funeral," and a few people laughed.
That line played in her head as she fed the buffaloes. It played again at dinner. Two days later, when Jatin said, "Everyone's still talking about your poem," she said, "Yeah, about how boring I was."
"What? No!"
She shrugged and went inside. She had already decided not to enter the district competition.

qa.q: What did Jatin shout from the back?
qa.a: Jatin shouted "Superstar!" from the back.

qa.q: Why does the mocking line feel more true to Amandeep than all the praise?
qa.a: The comment felt like a threat to how people see her, so her mind keeps replaying it, while the handshake, the teacher's tears and Jatin's cheering feel easy to shrug off.

qa.q: What went wrong in Amandeep's decision, and what could help before the district deadline?
qa.a: She let one comment decide she was boring and dropped the competition; talking it over with her teacher or Jatin and listing the real reactions might help her decide fairly.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel when Amandeep says people were talking about how boring she was?
qa.a: Jatin is likely confused and hurt for her, since Jatin knows the praise was real and can't understand why one stranger's joke counts more.

grounding: It shows a teenager replaying one mocking comment for days and shrugging off warm praise, which distorts how she sees herself.

passage:
Lars, sixteen, had three drawings in the school art show in Gothenburg: charcoal studies of his grandfather's hands. By the end of the evening his art teacher had called them "the most honest work in the room". A parent had asked if one was for sale. His friend Daniel had taken a photo and posted it with a row of hearts.
Then, near the drinks table, he heard a boy from another class say, "Looks like a kid drew it."
On the tram home, Daniel was still talking about the parent. Lars was staring out of the window, hearing "a kid drew it" again and again. At home he took the sketchbook out, looked at the hands, and thought they looked clumsy now.
For the next three days he didn't draw. When Daniel asked why, he said, "Guess I'm not that good." Daniel stared at him. "Were you even at the same show as me?"

qa.q: What did Lars's art teacher call his drawings?
qa.a: "The most honest work in the room."

qa.q: Why does one remark make Lars see his drawings as clumsy?
qa.a: Lars feels hurt and discouraged, because the critical line seems like the real truth about his skill, so it drowns out the teacher, the parent and Daniel.

qa.q: What could Lars do to get a fairer picture of how the show went?
qa.a: He could write down every reaction he heard that night, good and bad, and then look at the whole list before deciding whether he is "good".

qa.q: How does Daniel see the same evening differently?
qa.a: Daniel remembers it as a success, the teacher's praise and a parent wanting to buy, so he can't believe Lars thinks he isn't good.

grounding: It shows a teenager replaying one mocking comment for days and shrugging off warm praise, which dents his sense of his own worth.

passage: Disha, you've been staring at that one comment on your video for three days, haven't you? Let your Seema masi tell you something. When I was fifteen, I sang at the school annual day. Afterwards the principal praised me, my friends hugged me, and my music teacher said I had a real voice. But on the way out, a boy from Class 11 said, "She sounds like a pressure cooker." I heard that line in my head every night for weeks. I stopped singing, even at home. My friend Shobha kept telling me how much she missed my songs, and I just shrugged. Then, a year later, Shobha asked me to sing at her sister's wedding. I said yes only for her. When the whole courtyard sang along, I realised I had let one boy decide for everyone.

qa.q: What did the boy from Class 11 say about Seema's singing?
qa.a: He said, 'She sounds like a pressure cooker.'

qa.q: Why did young Seema shrug off Shobha's praise?
qa.a: Seema felt hurt and ashamed, and that one mocking line had grown so loud in her head that the warm words didn't seem to count.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Seema's story?
qa.a: Saying yes to singing at Shobha's sister's wedding; when the courtyard sang along, she saw she had let one boy's mockery outweigh everyone else.

qa.q: How might Shobha have felt during the year Seema stopped singing?
qa.a: Shobha missed the songs and probably felt sad and a little helpless that her praise wasn't getting through.

grounding: Shows a teenager replaying one mocking comment for weeks while shrugging off warm praise from friends and teachers.

passage: Salma had won the inter-school debate on Friday. Her team hugged her, the judge called her closing "fearless", and her class group filled up with clapping. But at the bus stop, Pankaj from the rival school had muttered, "Fake. All drama, no facts." Now it was Monday, the board practice exam was the next morning, and the bus to her tuition was crawling through wedding traffic, horns blaring. Salma had her physics notes open on her lap. She hadn't read a line. "All drama, no facts," she kept hearing, over the horns. Her best friend texted, "Still can't believe how good you were!!" Salma typed "thanks" and turned the phone face down. She pressed her forehead to the window and wondered if everyone secretly agreed with Pankaj.

qa.q: What did the judge call Salma's closing?
qa.a: The judge called it 'fearless'.

qa.q: Why did Salma turn her phone face down after her friend's message?
qa.a: Salma felt hurt and unsure of herself, and Pankaj's comment was so loud in her mind that praise felt hard to believe, even from her best friend.

qa.q: What could Salma do to stop one comment from taking over before the exam?
qa.a: She could write down the judge's word, her team's hugs and her friend's message next to Pankaj's line, remember that Pankaj was from the rival school, and talk it through with someone she trusts.

qa.q: How might Salma's best friend feel getting only 'thanks' back?
qa.a: The friend might feel puzzled or a little worried, having sent real excitement and received a flat reply.

grounding: Shows a teenager replaying one mocking remark for days and brushing off warm praise, which starts to shake her sense of herself.

passage: Yusuf posted his sketch of Charminar at dusk on the school art page on Saturday. By Sunday it had thirty-one comments. "Wow," "the light is amazing," "print this!" One said: "lol my baby cousin draws better." By Tuesday, Yusuf had read that one maybe fifty times. He had not reread the others once. In the canteen, Jeevan scrolled through them aloud. "Listen: 'the shadows look real.' 'Teach me please.'" Yusuf shrugged, eyes on his tiffin. "They're just being nice. That guy was being honest." "Or that guy was bored," Jeevan said. That night, Yusuf's thumb hovered over 'delete post' for a long time. Then he took a screenshot of the kind comments first and saved it in a folder he named 'read these too'.

qa.q: How many comments did Yusuf's sketch get by Sunday?
qa.a: It had thirty-one comments by Sunday.

qa.q: Why does Yusuf call the mocking comment honest and the kind ones 'just being nice'?
qa.a: Yusuf feels hurt and doubtful, and his mind treats the one sting as the truth while the thirty kind comments seem easy to wave away.

qa.q: Why is the 'read these too' folder a good step?
qa.a: It keeps the kind comments where Yusuf can see them, so the record stays balanced instead of one comment deciding how good the drawing is.

qa.q: How does Jeevan see the comments?
qa.a: Jeevan sees thirty kind comments worth reading aloud, and thinks the mean one came from someone who was just bored.

grounding: Shows a teenager replaying one mocking comment for days and shrugging off warm praise, starting to doubt his own worth.

passage: Last spring, someone in my class called my singing "like a pressure-cooker whistle." I'm Yamini, and I still remember the exact tone. It was one boy, once, at lunch. That same week, the music teacher chose me for the school choir solo. Tenzin, my best friend, said my voice gave her goosebumps. Three girls from Class 9 asked me to teach them the song. And I can barely remember their faces. I only replayed the pressure cooker, again and again, for days. I almost refused the solo. Looking back, I think my brain treated that one comment like a danger sign and filed the nice ones as background noise. Tenzin finally made me write down every kind thing people said that week. There were eleven. I stuck the list inside my music folder. I sang the solo.

qa.q: How many kind things did Yamini write down that week?
qa.a: There were eleven.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling during the days she replayed the comment?
qa.a: Yamini felt hurt and doubtful, so shaken by the one mocking comment that the solo almost got refused.

qa.q: What did Tenzin suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: Writing down every kind thing said that week, which made the eleven good comments as solid as the one mean one.

qa.q: How does Tenzin see Yamini's singing?
qa.a: Tenzin loves it, saying Yamini's voice gives her goosebumps.

grounding: A teenager looks back on replaying one mocking comment about Yamini's singing for days while shrugging off warm praise from many people.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 10B, 16 August.
Neelam has seemed low since Monday. Today she told me why. At the debate practice, a boy muttered that her English "sounded like a village girl." She has thought about it every day since.
I asked what else people said at the practice. She shrugged. So I read her the feedback forms I had collected. The judges wrote that her argument was the strongest. Her teammates wrote "fearless" and "clear." Seven positive notes, one unkind mutter.
She said, "But the mutter felt real." I understand. Hurtful words stick harder. I have spoken to the boy separately about the remark. With Neelam, I suggested she keep the feedback forms and read them before the next debate. She took them home.

qa.q: How many positive notes were on the feedback forms?
qa.a: Seven positive notes, one unkind mutter.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling since Monday?
qa.a: She felt low and hurt, thinking every day about the one unkind remark about her English.

qa.q: What did the teacher do, and why was it helpful?
qa.a: The teacher read Neelam the positive feedback, spoke to the boy separately about the remark, and suggested she reread the forms before the next debate.

qa.q: How did Neelam's teammates see her at the practice?
qa.a: Her teammates saw her as fearless and clear, the opposite of what the unkind remark suggested.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a teenager replaying one mocking comment for days while overlooking warm praise from judges and teammates.

passage:
The whole kasba turned out when Ritu came home with the silver medal from the district 800 metres. The shopkeeper gave her free jalebis. Her PT teacher put her photo on the school board. Irfan, who trained with her every morning on the canal road, told everyone it was her best time.
But at the bus stand, a boy from the next village had smirked, "Silver? You were so slow at the end, even my grandmother would have passed you."
For three days, that was the only race Ritu remembered. She skipped morning training. She stopped wearing the medal.
On the fourth morning, Irfan knocked on her door holding a notebook. "Your times since January," he said. "Every week, faster. One boy saw the last twenty metres. I saw all of it."
Ritu looked at the numbers for a long time. Then she went to get her shoes.

qa.q: In which race did Ritu win silver?
qa.a: Ritu won silver in the district 800 metres.

qa.q: Why did Ritu skip morning training for three days?
qa.a: Ritu felt humiliated and deflated, and the boy's mocking comment outweighed all the praise from the kasba.

qa.q: What did Irfan bring, and why did it help?
qa.a: A notebook of Ritu's times since January, showing steady improvement, which balanced one comment about the last twenty metres.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel watching Ritu stop training?
qa.a: Irfan is likely worried and a bit frustrated, having seen all of Ritu's hard work, and wants her to see it too.

grounding: Shows a teenager replaying one mocking remark for days and shrugging off a town's praise, until a friend shows the full record.

Her choir teacher said she had never sounded better. But in the hallway, a boy from her grade had grinned and said, "Nice. Sounded like a cat on the ice rink." For the next three days, while snow piled up against the windows, that line played in her head on repeat. At lunch Hana said, "Everyone loved it, Esther." Esther shrugged. "People just say that." That night she deleted the video from her phone without watching it again.
